notes.meaning: Laban's sons were jealous of Jacob's growing wealth. They spoke as if Jacob had robbed their father, but that was not true, since Laban still had large flocks of his own. Greedy people feel robbed by anything that goes to someone else. Even an honest person cannot always keep a good name.

Laban said little, but his face showed that he had turned against Jacob. Envy often shows on the face. Sour looks can ruin the peace of a family. The sons spoke their anger out loud, while their father kept quiet and let his face give him away.

Life with Laban was hard, yet Jacob would not leave until God told him to. God had brought him there, and now God sent him home with a promise: "I will be with you." Jacob would hold on to this promise later, when he was afraid of meeting Esau (32:9). Canaan is called the land of his fathers because God had promised it to them.

Jacob called Rachel and Leah out to the field so they could talk in private, away from Laban's household. A loving husband shares his plans with his wife. Only Rachel and Leah were called, because the other two wives were still servants.

Jacob told his wives two things: their father had turned against him, but God had stood by him. "The God of my father" means the God his family had always worshipped. In this way Jacob set the true God apart from the gods of Laban's house.
Jacob reminded his wives that he had worked hard and honestly for their father. They had seen it for themselves. Even when others do not do right by us, it is a comfort to know we did right by them.

Laban kept changing the deal to cheat Jacob. "Ten times" most likely means "many times," a round number for "over and over." Yet God did not let Laban really harm him. Those who stay close to God are kept safe by him.

Every time Laban changed the rule about which young animals Jacob could keep, the flock began giving birth to exactly that kind. It was as if Laban thought he could outsmart God himself. No natural cause could have matched every change without failing once, so God must have been behind it.

Jacob gives God the credit for his wealth. God took Laban's animals and gave them to Jacob as fair pay for his hard work. Later God did something similar for Israel, who left Egypt carrying the Egyptians' riches. Jacob's success came from God's command, not from cheating.

Jacob tells of a dream he had at breeding time. In it, the males mating with the flock all had the markings that meant Jacob's pay. Jacob had used his own clever methods, but the dream showed that God's blessing was what really mattered.

In the dream the angel of God called Jacob by name, and Jacob answered that he was ready to listen. The angel showed him that his success was not luck or his own skill. God had seen everything Laban did to him and was making it right. It is not clear exactly when this dream happened, because chapter 30 does not mention it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the differences between this account and chapter 30 show the story was put together from different written sources. Others answer that the difference simply reflects what Jacob chose to tell his wives.

notes.meaning: The angel speaks as God himself: "I am the God of Bethel." This reminded Jacob of the promise God made to him there, and of the vow (a solemn promise) Jacob made back. The Geneva Notes say this angel was Christ. Calvin says either God showed himself in this form or the angel spoke on God's behalf. Now God tells Jacob to go home, because even when the world smiles on us, it is not our true home.

Rachel and Leah agreed at once. They felt their father had treated them like outsiders, not daughters. He had in effect "sold" them for Jacob's years of work. Then he kept the profit for himself and gave them no share or inheritance.

The wives said the wealth God had moved from Laban to Jacob belonged to them and their children. They told Jacob to do whatever God had said. Wives who are true helpers never hold their husbands back from what God calls them to do. Calvin adds that their reasons were a bit worldly, since they spoke more of their rights than of God's blessing.

Once his wives agreed, Jacob moved quickly. He put his family on camels and drove his flocks toward his father Isaac in Canaan. He took only what was his own, the animals he had earned. He did not try to make up for his losses by taking anything of Laban's.

While Laban was away shearing sheep, Rachel stole his household idols, small images used in worship or to seek guidance. Rachel was not as honest as her husband. Matthew Henry hopes she took them to show her father how foolish it was to trust gods that could not protect themselves. Calvin thinks she simply still clung to these idols from her childhood.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some point to ancient clay tablets found at Nuzi that link such household idols to inheritance and property rights. On that reading, Rachel may have thought owning them would support Jacob's claim to the flocks.

notes.meaning: "Deceived" is literally "stole the heart." It means Jacob left without Laban knowing. Leaving suddenly was right, because God had told him to go and he was in danger. It was also wise, since Laban might have stopped him by force or robbed him.

differ.view: Sneaking away showed that Jacob still leaned on his own cleverness instead of fully trusting God's promise to be with him.

notes.meaning: Jacob fled with everything he owned, crossed the Euphrates River, and headed for the hills of Gilead, about 300 miles from Haran. It is not clear how he crossed the river with his flocks. There may have been well-known shallow places to cross. The hills were probably not called Gilead until after the events later in this chapter.

Laban did not hear about it for three days, because his shearing was three days' journey away. Calvin sees God's care in this head start. It let Jacob get across the river before Laban could chase him.

Laban gathered his relatives and chased Jacob for seven days. He moved fast, while Jacob was slowed by children and flocks. Laban meant to drag Jacob back or strip him of what he had. Bad people often work harder for their anger than good people do for their love.

The night before Laban caught up, God warned him in a dream. "Say nothing, good or bad" means "don't try to stop Jacob or turn him back." God tied Laban's hands even though he did not change his heart. Good people are often kept safe because God has a hold on the consciences of the wicked.
Laban caught up with Jacob in the hill country of Gilead, and both camped there. These hills formed the eastern edge of Canaan, so Jacob was already close to the promised land.

Laban accused Jacob of tricking him and carrying off his daughters like prisoners of war. He said nothing about his sons' complaint from verse 1. People who mean harm themselves are quick to put the worst spin on what others do.

Laban claimed he would have thrown a farewell party with songs, tambourines and harps, and that Jacob had robbed him of the chance to kiss his grandchildren goodbye. Given how he had treated Jacob, this was empty talk. When people cannot do the harm they planned, they pretend they meant only kindness. Matthew Henry also notes that Rebekah had been sent off from this family with prayers and blessings, not just merrymaking.
